name: Club percussion
credit: Virtuosity Drums — Versilian Studios and Karoryfer Samples (auxiliary percussion from VSCO 2 Pro)
_what: The percussionist. Ten voices out of the twenty-nine auxiliary percussion
maps Virtuosity ships, which came into that library from VSCO 2 Pro and
were recorded and mapped separately from Austin McMahon's kit — four mic
positions, the same names, a different room.
This is not a drum kit and is not loaded as one. The engine plays this
folder UNDER whichever kit the jam has chosen, so the set has to sit
against a drummer it cannot see: the balance is measured against the club
kit's snare accent (`balance_ref`), which is the same reference every kit
voice is already levelled against, so a number here means what the same
The nineteen maps left behind are agogo, belltree, cuica, jinglebell,
sleighbells, timbales, triangle, vibraslap, whistle, woodblock and the
fast guiro. They are not worse recordings; they are not the ten
instruments a percussionist reaches for in latin, funk, pop and world
grooves, which is what this layer is for. The contract names the ten.

_mic_tag: The percussion writes the mic at the END of the file name as a word
(`..._rr1_Overhead.wav`) where the drums write it at the front as the
directory's own name (`oh_snare_buzz_vl7.flac`). Without this table the
close mic is never found for any stroke, the mix silently drops the
channel it was weighted for, and the set is thin for no visible reason.

_stereo: swap_stereo is OFF here and it is ON for the drums, and that is not an
inconsistency. The kit is swapped because its overheads were imaged from
in front of the kit and the brief wants the drummer's seat — one honest
channel swap turns the whole kit round at once. The percussion is a
different recording of a different room by different hands, and there is
no drummer's seat to put anyone in.
Measured on the source, the percussion overheads are nearly centred: the
widest instrument sits 4.6 dB right and the narrowest 0.2 dB left. So the
files carry a little real width and nothing that could be called a
placement, and the placement is `pan` in the manifest — where the owner
can argue with it without a re-render. Seven of the ten pans agree with
the direction the room already leaned; the tambourine and the guiro are
asked to cross about 1 dB of it, which a 0.3 pan swamps.
_mix: The overheads lead and the close mic follows, which is the opposite of
the kick and the snare and is right for the reason those are not: a
percussionist is heard in the room, and a close mic on a shaker is a
recording of a hand. Every instrument here has all four mics, which the
cymbals and toms in `club.json` do not.
Two mixes. The struck and shaken metal and wood — shaker, tambourine,
cowbell, cabasa, claves, guiro — cut through anything and want air more
than proximity, so the close mic is at 0.45. The congas and the bongos
are drums with heads, and the body of a head is in the close mic, so they
get 0.7 — still under the overheads, because a conga mixed like a kick
arrives in front of the drummer instead of beside them.
_balance: dB against the club kit's snare accent, K-weighted over 400 ms, exactly
as the kits are balanced. The contract sets these and they are the
numbers to argue with when the owner says 'less shaker': the tool
measures what it got and writes the difference into trim_db, so the files
never change when the balance does.
A percussionist is quieter than a drummer and these say so. The shaker
and the cabasa sit 12 dB under the snare because they play every
sixteenth and anything louder is a hiss over the whole groove; the congas
are only 4 dB down because a conga tumbao is a melody and not a texture.

_: shaker_up and shaker_down are the two round robins of one voice,
because a shaker alternates by nature and the up-stroke and the
down-stroke are the two halves of one motion. In the source the
up-stroke is 8 to 11 dB quieter, which is the instrument and not the
session; peak normalisation lands both at 0.900, so what alternates
in the kit is the timbre of the two strokes, which is what you hear.
One layer. Each articulation is sampled at a single dynamic and its
seven shakes span 4.6 dB (up) and 1.6 dB (down) — the down-stroke has
no second layer in it, and a layer the library does not have cannot
be invented. A shaker's accent is in the hand, which is the gain.
One velocity band and ten shakes in it, spanning 8.2 dB — a wider
range than several instruments here that were sampled in bands. So
the round robins are ranked by loudness and stand in for the layers;
see `rank_rr_as_dynamics`.

cabasa._: Two dynamics, 12.1 dB apart. Two layers, and both of them real.

_: `guiro_slow` only. The contract skips `guiro_fast` because it is a
different stroke and not a louder one — a fast scrape is a shorter
instrument, and a groove that wants one wants it written into the
part, not reached by hitting the guiro harder.
One layer, for the same reason as the shaker: one dynamic, and its
eight scrapes span 3.7 dB, under the 4.5 dB step a second layer would
have to be worth.
1.0 s and not the 0.6 s the brief guessed at. A scrape is not a decay:
cutting it is not landing a tail, it is lifting the stick halfway
through the stroke, and 0.6 s did exactly that on every file. Measured,
the slow scrape runs 0.97 s, which is also about how long a cha-cha
wants it — beats one and two at 120.
`conga_muted` is layer 1 — the ghost stroke, a palm laid on the head
— and `conga_open` supplies the two above it. No velocity of an open
stroke is that sound however softly it is struck, so this is an
articulation standing in for a velocity band, which is what
`combine: layers` is for. The engine plays layer 1 on a ghost, so the
muted stroke lands exactly where the contract puts it.
The tumba, the big drum of the set. Four dynamics in the source and
three taken; the softest band is left alone because one of its eight
strokes is 30 dB under its siblings and the band is not a performance
anyone would play.
